records.name: Abscopal effect
records.tldr: An abscopal response is regression outside an irradiated area, studied as a possible systemic effect of local radiation. Observing it does not by itself establish the cause or an added survival benefit.
records.summary:
Responses at non-irradiated sites motivate investigation of immune effects of local radiation. Keep the irradiated and unirradiated lesions, other treatments and observation times explicit. A proposed immune mechanism needs more than local injury or circulating markers.

A case or uncontrolled combination cannot isolate the added effect of radiation. Comparative local-treatment studies must retain their populations and endpoints: a response outside the field, progression-free survival, overall survival and symptom relief are different outcomes.

notes: First define the irradiated field and the actual exposure of each lesion. A local response does not demonstrate a distant response. An uninjected-lesion response in an injection study is a different route-defined observation. During concurrent systemic treatment, distant shrinkage does not by itself isolate radiation’s contribution or demonstrate immune causation; local control, distant response, survival, symptoms and harms require separate assessment.

Demaria’s bilateral 67NR mammary-tumour mouse experiment combined local radiation with Flt3 ligand. The distant tumour grew more slowly under the combination, whereas radiation alone affected the irradiated tumour; antigen-mismatched and T-cell-deficient comparisons supported an immune-dependent component. This is a defined combined animal intervention, not a human response rate. Postow’s ipilimumab-plus-radiation melanoma report was one case with temporal immune correlates, not a study of frequency.

Formenti enrolled 39 people with chemotherapy-refractory metastatic non-small-cell lung cancer in a single-arm radiation-plus-ipilimumab study. At day 88, 21 had completed treatment and response assessment. Seven responses were 7/39, about 18% of those enrolled, or 7/21, about 33% of those evaluable. Seventeen received fewer than four cycles because they progressed or died before day 88; another completed four cycles without response assessment. These denominators answer different questions and neither estimates radiation-alone activity or an individual breast-cancer response probability.

To assess a distant effect, retain lesion exposure, serial imaging, prespecified response rules, timing and concurrent therapies. Report lesion changes separately from patient response proportions and their eligible denominators. Imaging is an input; optional tissue and immune tests use finite samples. Exposure misclassification, missing assessments, selected evaluable groups and concurrent-drug attribution can distort interpretation. There is no universal abscopal cutoff or percentage across cancers and regimens; case observations, model mechanisms and comparative clinical outcomes are different evidence tiers.

In a fictional combination study, an irradiated site is controlled while a lesion outside the field shrinks during systemic therapy. The observation is a distant response under that treatment context. It does not prove that radiation vaccinated the whole body, establish which component caused it or supply a general response frequency. Test exposure, relevant comparisons and the proposed immune mechanism separately.

Ho's single-arm phase 2 study combined radiation with pembrolizumab in metastatic triple-negative breast cancer. The week-13 unirradiated-lesion endpoint yielded three responses among seventeen enrolled people, 17.6%, with a 95% confidence interval of 4.7% to 44.2%. Eight died from progression before week 13; among the nine assessed then, the same three responses were 33.3%, rounded to one decimal place. These are different denominators for the same numerator, not two treatment effects. Without a randomised systemic-treatment-only group, neither proportion estimates what radiation added or supplies a general abscopal probability.

records.name: Immunogenic cell death
records.tldr: Immunogenic cell death is regulated cell death that can initiate adaptive immunity against the dying cells in a suitable host and context. Injury alone does not establish it.
records.summary:
The 2020 consensus defines immunogenic cell death through the adaptive immune response, not merely the appearance of dead cells. Antigens, appropriately timed danger signals, antigen-presenting cells and a responsive host all matter. Apoptotic or other death machinery does not by itself classify the immune outcome.

Calreticulin exposure, ATP or HMGB1 release and interferon-related signals are useful mechanistic readouts, but none alone proves protective immunity. Functional cross-priming and appropriate in-vivo immune tests address later steps. The consensus distinguishes mouse vaccination models from established disease; neither a surrogate marker nor a positive mouse assay establishes clinical benefit in a person.

notes: In a local-treatment study, follow injury and signals through presentation, priming, recognition and measured tumour outcomes. Circulating cytokines or proliferating T cells alone do not establish tumour-specific killing, distant control or an optimal radiation dose.

Immunogenic cell death is regulated death capable of initiating antigen-specific adaptive immunity in a compatible responding host. Antigenicity and appropriately timed adjuvant signals are both necessary considerations. It is an immune consequence, not an exclusive machine opposed to apoptosis or necrotic appearance.

Surface calreticulin, released ATP and HMGB1 have distinct mechanistic roles in defined experiments. Calreticulin supported dying-cell uptake, ATP signalled through dendritic-cell P2X7/inflammasome pathways, and HMGB1/TLR4 supported processing and presentation. These are examples rather than a universal sufficient three-marker checklist. A DAMP is not automatically a tumour-specific antigen.

In the consensus vaccination assay, remove residual inducing chemical and add no separate adjuvant before vaccinating immunocompetent syngeneic mice with dying tumour cells. Compare later challenge with living matched tumour cells in vaccinated and unvaccinated hosts, and test specificity with unrelated compatible tumour cells. Incidence and growth are functional readouts. Immune-competent versus deficient comparisons alone cannot isolate immunogenic death from other immunostimulation. Assays consume tumour-cell aliquots, supernatant or host-model material and report separate dead-cell fractions, signal concentrations or surface staining and challenge incidence or growth. Residual inducer, contamination, incompatible antigens and poor death confirmation can invalidate attribution. No universal DAMP cutoff establishes immunogenicity.

Death plus extracellular ATP does not establish a cancer vaccine. Danger signals, cross-priming, functional protection, distant control and patient benefit are separate claims. Even a positive mouse vaccination assay remains model-bound and does not select a clinical treatment.

records.name: In situ vaccination
records.tldr: In situ vaccination aims to use antigens at a tumour site to stimulate useful immune recognition. Local destruction does not automatically make the tumour a successful vaccine.
records.summary:
Local treatment can supply tumour antigens, and an adjuvant or other immune intervention may support their presentation and priming. The proposal needs evidence for each step and for useful immune effects in the relevant host and setting. It does not guarantee recognition of every antigen or every lesion.

Injury, danger signals, immune-cell changes, distant lesion responses and comparative patient outcomes are different observations. The actual local method and accompanying treatments must be named. A response during combined treatment does not isolate which component caused it.

notes: The strategy uses relevant tumour antigens in place while supporting presenting cells and immune activation. Antigen availability, uptake and processing, cross-presentation, suitable priming, access to another lesion, recognition of naturally displayed targets and useful function are conditional jobs. Local injury can supply material without establishing all these steps, and danger signals alone do not establish immunogenic cell death. An uninjected lesion can still be exposed to systemic drugs.

Intratumoral immunotherapy describes a delivery route and treatment purpose; in-situ vaccination describes a proposed learning strategy. Not every injected cytotoxic or immune-directed treatment is a vaccine. Local shrinkage, antigen-reactive blood responses, distant control and longer-term clinical benefit are different outcomes, and a multicomponent result does not isolate each component’s contribution.

Brody’s early study combined low-dose radiation and an injected CpG TLR9 agonist in 15 people with low-grade B-cell lymphoma. Hammerich combined Flt3 ligand, radiation and the TLR3 agonist poly-ICLC in indolent lymphoma with accompanying models. The latter report’s restored sensitivity to PD-1 blockade was demonstrated in mice; it is not established human combination benefit or evidence for every injection or a breast-cancer regimen.

Assessment combines local sampling, controlled immune assays and serial treated/uninjected-lesion measurements. Tissue, blood and viable cells are finite inputs. Keep local change, specified reactive-cell counts or functions, and response proportions under their stated rules separate. No universal marker proves successful vaccination. Nonspecific inflammation, added peptide, viability, missed sampling times and concurrent therapy can confound results; a model or assay needs separate clinical validation of the complete intervention.

Added peptide can bypass natural processing. Appropriate naturally presenting targets and recognition or cytotoxicity controls address a separate bridge, within the model’s limits. In a fictional study, the injected lesion shrinks and blood cells respond to supplied tumour peptides, while another lesion is unchanged. Local activity and assay reactivity were observed; natural recognition, access and useful distant function remain unproven. The unchanged lesion also does not establish absence of every immune-learning event.

For T-cell-directed therapeutic strategies, compare the antigen source and what can be selected beforehand. An in-situ approach uses tumour material in the body and selects a site and intervention; a supplied design selects planned composition or encoded targets using adequate sample information or material. Defined peptide or encoded targets differ from broader cell preparations. Manufacturing a product does not mean every peptide ultimately displayed is known or controlled. The room-material versus teaching-kit analogy describes these inputs, not assured learning or a winner.

Priming is initial activation of a naive T cell. Cross-presentation places externally acquired material on class I HLA in a presenting cell; that event is distinct from a cancer cell naturally displaying a recognised target. Both strategies still need evidence of presentation, suitable priming or expansion, tumour access, useful function, outcomes and harms. Dashed links in a comparison diagram mark questions to investigate, not successful completion of each step.

The required opportunity depends on the method. A lesion-based local approach needs available tumour material at an identified, safely accessible site. A supplied product needs appropriate information or material and a workable manufacturing and delivery plan. If no identifiable lesion is accessible, that removes the stated opportunity for that local method; it does not show that another vaccine is feasible or choose treatment. Match a research question about local material and support to that design, or one about planned antigen selection to a supplied design, then compare complete strategies in suitable studies.

Injection specifies a route, and using one person's tumour material is not equivalent to manufacturing a selected personalised vaccine. A study can combine local tumour material with a supplied antigen product; report both sources rather than forcing one exclusive category. Personalisation, platform and route are independent descriptors. Local shrinkage, an immune assay and control at another lesion remain different outcomes.

Consider two fictional cards. A uses accessible tumour material with a local intervention and immune stimulus; B supplies selected encoded targets based on sample information. Neither gives outcome data. A does not specify a fixed presented mixture, and B does not guarantee processing, HLA display or natural tumour recognition. For both, investigate presentation, priming, access and function and then matched clinical outcomes and harms. If A's lesion becomes inaccessible, B is not thereby chosen. If B is added to A, the study now uses both antigen sources.

The examples answer different questions. Brody used radiation plus injected CpG in low-grade lymphoma. Hammerich used Flt3 ligand, low-dose radiation and poly-ICLC in indolent lymphoma, with accompanying models; the reported new responsiveness to PD-1 blockade was in mice. Ott's melanoma study supplied selected long peptides with poly-ICLC. These are not a head-to-head efficacy ranking, evidence for a breast-cancer regimen or an individual eligibility assessment.

records.name: Dendritic-cell cross-presentation (cDC1)
records.tldr: Cross-presentation displays externally acquired protein fragments on class I HLA. Initial activation of a naive T cell is a further step called cross-priming.
records.summary:
Class I HLA commonly displays fragments of proteins made within the presenting cell. Cross-presentation means displaying externally acquired antigen on class I HLA. Naive CD8 T-cell priming is a further activation step requiring an appropriate presenting cell and supporting signals; tumour-cell display alone does not establish priming. The subset specialised for this is the type 1 conventional dendritic cell (cDC1): CD8alpha+ and CD103+ in mice, CD141 (BDCA-3)+ in humans, dependent on FLT3 ligand and the transcription factor BATF3 for development, internalising necrotic-cell material through CLEC9A (DNGR-1), a receptor for polymerised actin, and expressing the chemokine receptor XCR1, which favours contact with CD8 T cells (Alfaro et al., 2013).

The in vivo proof came from Batf3-deficient mice (Hildner et al., Science 2008): they lacked CD8alpha+ dendritic cells, their dendritic cells were defective in cross-presentation, and they failed to reject highly immunogenic syngeneic tumours. In mouse melanoma, CD103+ dendritic cells were the only antigen-presenting cells carrying intact antigen to lymph nodes and priming tumour-specific CD8 T cells, and they were required for PD-L1 blockade to work; expanding them with FLT3 ligand and activating them with intratumoral poly I:C improved responses to PD-L1 and BRAF inhibition (Salmon et al., Immunity 2016). This is why a scarcity of cDC1 in a tumour is read as one cause of a cold, checkpoint-resistant tumour, and why vaccine designs target antigen to cDC1 receptors such as CLEC9A, or expand and activate these cells, rather than relying on bulk monocyte-derived dendritic cells.

Cross-presentation names a display process, whereas cross-priming names the activation of naive CD8 T cells through it, which needs supporting signals and its own readout. Direct presentation remains possible: a dendritic cell that receives vaccine messenger RNA and makes the protein itself presents it directly. A cell can also acquire already assembled peptide-HLA complexes from another cell (cross-dressing), which does not show processing by the recipient (Wakim and Bevan, Nature 2011, PMID 21455179, mouse viral infection). External antigen on class II is not cross-presentation.

records.name: T-cell priming and the three-signal model
records.tldr: A naive T cell's first activation depends on recognition and supporting signals. Division and killing are separate outcomes.
records.summary:
The three-signal teaching model groups peptide-HLA recognition by the T-cell receptor as signal one, costimulation as signal two and cytokine context as signal three. The naive cell already has its receptor. The model organises interacting processes; it is not a universal three-step checklist, and experienced or engineered cells can have different requirements.

Curtsinger and colleagues showed that type I interferons or IL-12 could support naive CD8 survival and effector differentiation in defined experiments. Proliferation without a third signal did not establish cytolytic function. Antigen presentation and initial priming are different processes. In a fictional matched comparison, two cultures each divide three times but only one kills appropriate targets above target-only background: equal division does not show equal function. Compare viable-cell input, peptide loading, HLA compatibility, cell ratios, exposure and positive and negative controls. Priming does not itself demonstrate natural tumour display, tumour access, safe killing or patient benefit.

notes: Priming is a naive cell's initial activation in a supporting context. Signal one is TCR recognition of peptide-HLA, signal two includes CD80/CD86-CD28 costimulation and inhibitory context, and signal three includes differentiation-supporting cytokines. The receptor pre-exists the encounter. These signals interact over time; the model is not a three-button checklist and antigen-experienced or engineered cells can have different requirements.

IL-12 and type I interferons (alpha/beta) supported naive CD8 survival and cytolytic differentiation in defined experiments. Cytokines are signalling proteins, not nutritional fuel. Type I interferon can connect innate responses to priming, but this does not prescribe a universal cytokine intervention or establish every cGAS-STING step. Dendritic-cell priming support and tumour antigen display answer different questions.

Division, viable-cell expansion, cytokine production and target-cell death are distinct priming outcomes. In a fictional matched experiment both cultures show three divisions, yet only B kills appropriate targets above target-only background. Measure these outcomes separately with defined starting cells, presenting system, signal perturbation, matched time, peptide loading, HLA, cell ratios and culture conditions. Priming does not establish tumour access, natural display, safe killing or clinical benefit, and stronger stimulation can support unwanted populations.

records.name: T-cell receptor
records.tldr: A conventional T-cell receptor recognises a peptide together with its HLA display. Recognition alone does not show killing.
records.summary:
A conventional alpha-beta T-cell receptor uses paired chains to recognise a peptide-HLA surface. Its recognition chains assemble with CD3 signalling partners, as demonstrated in the human TCR-CD3 structural study. CDR3 is an informative variable region, but neither a beta-chain sequence nor CDR3 alone specifies the complete paired receptor or its function.

Particular receptors can cross-react across peptide and HLA contexts; that does not establish a universal cross-reactivity rate. Paired receptor identity, binding, activation, target-cell death and clinical benefit require different evidence. A response by one reconstructed pair to peptide-loaded cells does not establish that another alpha-chain pairing recognises the same target, or that either kills naturally presenting tumour cells. Use irrelevant-target, HLA and target-only viability controls. Peptide loading can bypass natural processing, and contact diagrams are not healthy-tissue safety tests.

notes: A conventional alpha-beta TCR uses paired variable and constant domains to contact peptide plus HLA. The peptide sits in the HLA groove, not a separate TCR peptide pocket. CD3 signalling partners are distinct from recognition chains. Contact loops including junction-spanning CDR3 contribute, but other loops, the partner chain and HLA matter; beta-only or CDR3-only sequence is incomplete.

Cross-reactivity is recognition of multiple targets by a receptor. Defined receptor experiments demonstrated peptide/HLA cross-reactivity, not recognition of every allele by an arbitrary receptor or a universal rate. Greater affinity or a contact drawing does not establish healthy-tissue safety.

Sequencing reports sampled receptor identities and abundances under an operational clonotype definition. Paired alpha-beta identities are more complete than beta alone. Peptide-HLA multimer binding, stimulus-induced cellular response, target-cell death and clinical benefit are different endpoints. Include irrelevant-target, HLA and target-only viability controls; peptide-loaded cells can bypass natural processing.

Vaccination generally recruits or expands existing mature receptor specificities rather than rewriting each mature receptor. Engineered TCR therapy introduces selected receptor sequences. In either case, tested recognition must still connect to naturally presenting tumour targets, useful function and healthy-tissue safety. If one beta sequence pairs with different alpha chains, a positive reconstruction of one pair does not establish the other pair's function or tumour killing.

Source scope: teaching synthesis checked against the cited abstracts and specified accessible primary text on 9 November 2026; fictional examples are not clinical observations or treatment-selection rules.

Many measured conventional receptor-peptide-HLA interactions have micromolar dissociation constants; affinity, multiple contacts, CD4/CD8 coreceptors and the cellular signalling context contribute differently to activity. Stone and colleagues review those distinctions, rather than a universal affinity ranking against every antibody. One receptor type per cell is also a simplification: extra productive alpha chains and dual surface receptors have been documented. A chain sequence alone does not establish which assembled receptor provides the measured specificity.

records.name: Circulating tumour DNA (ctDNA)
records.tldr: Circulating tumour DNA (ctDNA) consists of fragments of DNA shed by tumour cells into the blood, detectable with sensitive sequencing.
records.summary: Circulating tumour DNA (ctDNA) is made up of DNA fragments shed by tumour cells into the bloodstream, where they form only a small fraction of all cell-free DNA and are detected with sensitive sequencing. Its uses span genotyping for companion diagnostics, tracking resistance mutations such as EGFR T790M and ESR1, molecular residual disease, early detection and response monitoring. Shedding varies with tumour type and burden, and clonal haematopoiesis can confound results. The term underpins the Liquid biopsy (ctDNA), MRD / molecular residual disease testing and Multi-cancer early detection (MCED) technologies, and it appears in the SERENA-6, CIRCULATE-Japan and IMvigor011 trials and in ideas on molecular-progression switching beyond ESR1 and HPV ctDNA to guide cervical cancer therapy.

notes: Detection depends on stage and tumour type: with digital PCR-based methods in 640 patients, ctDNA was found in more than 75% of people with advanced pancreatic, ovarian, colorectal, bladder, gastro-oesophageal, breast, melanoma, hepatocellular and head and neck cancers, and in fewer than 50% of primary brain, renal, prostate or thyroid cancers. In localised disease it was found in 73% of colorectal, 57% of gastro-oesophageal, 48% of pancreatic and 50% of breast adenocarcinomas, and it was often present in people with no detectable circulating tumour cells (Bettegowda 2014). The assay, specimen and population are part of each figure.

ctDNA is a subset of cell-free DNA, and not every plasma variant is tumour-derived: in paired plasma and white-blood-cell sequencing, 53.2% of cfDNA mutations in 124 people with metastatic cancer and 81.6% in 47 people without cancer had features of clonal haematopoiesis (Razavi 2019). A ctDNA result is also a quantity with a unit (molecules per millilitre, a fraction, or a call), and the same number means different things under each.

Lung cancer: plasma genotyping at diagnosis is non-inferior to tissue for finding a guideline biomarker (27.3% against 21.3% in 282 patients), has 100% positive predictive value for the alterations with approved drugs, returns in 9 days against 15, and raises detection by 48% when added to tissue (Leighl 2019). Clinical sensitivity against tissue is 80%, so a negative plasma result rules nothing out and the guideline permits plasma to rule in only (Lindeman 2018). Serial plasma after starting treatment also separates the patients whose resistant clone was already present, within three weeks (Oxnard 2018).

records.name: ctDNA and imaging discordance
records.tldr: A blood DNA result and an imaging result can seem to disagree because they sample different material, regions, times and signals. A mismatch is a question to resolve, not a verdict on either test.
records.summary:
A circulating tumour DNA (ctDNA) assay looks for tumour-associated features in a finite sample of cell-free DNA. How much tumour DNA reaches the sampled blood varies between lesions, and recovery, background DNA, the features tracked and the assay's detection limit all shape the call. Imaging measures a defined region through a physical signal. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the breast can report contrast enhancement or the volume of enhancing tissue, which is not a direct count of viable cancer cells. The two tests can therefore differ without either being wrong, and neither automatically replaces the other.

They can also share information. In Magbanua and colleagues' pilot of 84 women having neoadjuvant chemotherapy for early breast cancer, ctDNA concentration was correlated with MRI functional tumour volume at all four time points, with Spearman correlations of 0.42 to 0.49, and patients with detectable ctDNA had a higher median volume. Agreement was partial, and adding ctDNA early in treatment to volume-based prediction of pathological complete response gave only a numerical gain that was not statistically significant. ctDNA positivity after treatment added significantly to volume for predicting distant recurrence and death. A mismatch calls for checking dates, assay limits, the imaged region and the exact finding. It does not by itself show a false test or hidden metastatic disease.

notes: Method card, what is compared: a sampled molecular signal in plasma and a regional physical signal from a named imaging protocol. Their units, dates and thresholds stay separate, and the comparison is only as good as the date alignment of the two acquisitions.

Table, blood side: input is a blood draw and the plasma and recovered DNA analysed, and testing consumes an aliquot. Output is a qualifying call plus a defined concentration or fraction, read with the assay's detection and quantitation rules. Failure modes are low shedding, finite input, poor recovery and background or blood-cell variants.

Table, imaging side: input is the imaged region and a protocol, and contrast or tracer use depends on the modality. Output is size, volume, uptake or a qualitative finding read against protocol-specific response criteria. Failure modes are artefacts, non-tumour contributions to the signal and technique that differs between visits.

Table, what each cannot tell: blood alone cannot locate a lesion or give a cell count. Imaging alone cannot count viable tumour cells, and enhancement can have more than one tissue cause. Neither agreement nor disagreement shows that a treatment change would help, which is a clinical-utility question.

Evidence read: Magbanua's pilot (84 patients, MTM/mL against MRI functional tumour volume) found correlation at T0 to T3 with rho 0.49, 0.42, 0.42 and 0.43, and its authors call the findings preliminary in a limited cohort needing larger validation. It supports partial agreement and does not set a rule for redirecting treatment.

Interpretation rule, from finite sampling: a plasma aliquot can hold no tumour molecule when the true share is small, so no qualifying ctDNA signal alongside an abnormal MRI region does not show the region is only scar. The converse holds too: a clear image does not exclude tumour DNA in blood. Each result answers only its own question.

Source attribution comes first: a positive plasma variant may come from a blood-cell clone rather than a tumour. In Razavi's paired sequencing, 53.2% of cell-free DNA mutations in 124 people with metastatic cancer and 81.6% in 47 people without cancer had features of clonal haematopoiesis, so a discordant positive needs origin checks before it is read as occult disease.

Half-life, scoped: Diehl and colleagues estimated a ctDNA half-life after surgery of 114 minutes by evaluating one subject whose plasma was sampled at several early times after complete resection in a study of 162 plasma samples from 18 subjects with colorectal cancer (Diehl 2008). That is a single-subject estimate of post-resection clearance in colorectal cancer, not a universal cfDNA half-life, a breast-cancer figure or a blood-draw schedule. DNA release and clearance can change sooner than visible tissue structure, which is a reason to align the dates of the blood and imaging acquisitions.

Use the blood collection date and imaging acquisition date to compare biology, then keep the reporting dates as a separate measure of when the information became available. Imaging does not remove a tissue aliquot for molecular analysis; contrast or tracer use belongs to the specific protocol. Agreement can reflect shared dependence on disease burden and is not two independent proofs of the same mechanism. Combining measurements into a decision rule needs validation of the combination and its intended outcome.

In a fictional early-breast-cancer example, a negative plasma result is not an examination of the breast tumour bed or regional nodes. It cannot by itself establish pathological complete response or validate skipping surgery. Using a result to remove a treatment needs evidence for that decision strategy and its clinical outcomes, beyond showing that an assay can detect a signal. This is an interpretation limit, not a claim that no omission study exists.

The two-window comparison is about scope. A finite plasma aliquot contains extracellular DNA, of which tumour-derived fragments may be one part; breast MRI observes regional, sequence-dependent features rather than individual cancer cells. Contrast enhancement reflects vascular and contrast-delivery behaviour as well as the acquisition protocol; it is not a one-to-one viable-cell count. In the 84-person I-SPY2 MRI pilot, functional tumour volume summed voxels meeting 70% enhancement about two and a half minutes after contrast, inside a manually drawn box around the lesion. A camera-and-stream analogy illustrates those two sampled views without promising that every tumour sheds DNA. Keep the imaging method visible: mammography uses X-rays, ultrasound uses sound, and PET/CT combines tracer-distribution images with anatomical CT images. A formal response category needs its framework, comparison timepoint and findings outside a selected lesion measurement. None of these measurements is an interchangeable all-body tumour-cell number.

Four patterns illustrate the reading boundary. A smaller lesion and lower detected blood signal mean that both recorded measures fell in their own units, not that pCR or eradication of distant disease is proved. A residual scan finding with undetected blood leaves viability, treatment effects and other causes unresolved. Detected blood with no suspicious finding in the scanned region does not establish the signal's location, full extent or best intervention. If neither shows qualifying evidence, neither has proved zero microscopic disease or justified omitting indicated treatment. These are interpretation examples, not an action algorithm; disagreement alone does not establish pseudoprogression.

In a fictional course, a breast lesion becomes less enhancing, blood changes from detected to not detected, and surgery later finds residual invasive cancer. There is no contradiction: imaging features, a finite molecular sample and removed tissue answer different questions. Only the specified tissue assessment establishes the residual disease in this example. A smaller scan finding and undetected blood can therefore be favourable observations without confirming pCR. Conversely, a later positive blood result with clear regional breast imaging calls for review of sample qualification, origin, dates and clinical context; it is not itself a diagnosis of distant metastasis.

Magbanua and colleagues' 2025 analysis evaluated 723 high-risk I-SPY2 patients across hormone receptor-positive/HER2-negative, triple-negative and HER2-positive subtypes. Combining ctDNA with residual cancer burden refined prognostic groups, but analyses within those groups used smaller subsets, some too small for multivariable adjustment. The authors also found retained patient-specific assay variants in sampled resistant tumours from patients whose post-treatment plasma was negative. These results support studying risk information and shedding; they do not turn negative presurgical blood into tissue pCR or demonstrate that a blood-guided omission strategy improves outcomes.

Adding receptor measurements introduces another question to a blood and imaging comparison. A sequenced clonotype's sampled abundance does not directly measure its antigen, effector activity or total cell count. Even a controlled secretion or killing result belongs to its tested stimulus and targets. Collecting the measurements together does not link a particular receptor to the tumour DNA signal. Retain time, compartment, chain definition, abundance unit, controls and independent target-recognition evidence; combining the results does not make a validated treatment rule.

In a fictional comparison using compatible measurements, tumour DNA is stable or rising in two patterns and falls in two others, while a receptor measure changes little or increases. Stable or rising DNA with little repertoire change raises questions about the tumour, immunity and assay adequacy without diagnosing resistance or mandating a tissue or spatial test. With greater repertoire change it still does not prove a physical barrier or an antigen-specific response that failed. Falling DNA with little repertoire change does not assign the effect to chemotherapy or show that useful immunity is absent. Falling DNA with greater repertoire change does not prove that immune learning caused control. These are sampled observations, not validated best-response categories, proof of clinical benefit or instructions to change treatment.

records.name: ctDNA units, fractions and concentrations
records.tldr: A ctDNA result is a number with a unit. Molecules per millilitre, parts per million and allele fraction answer different questions, so a printed number means nothing until its unit and denominator are known.
records.summary:
Circulating tumour DNA (ctDNA) can be reported as a concentration, as a fraction, or as a yes or no call, and the three are not interchangeable. A concentration counts tumour-attributed molecules in a stated volume of plasma. One example is mean tumour molecules per millilitre (MTM/mL), which the I-SPY 2 breast-cancer study of Magbanua and colleagues used for ctDNA across tracked variants. A fraction divides tumour-attributed molecules by a stated total, such as all evaluated alleles at one position (variant allele fraction, VAF) or all evaluated DNA (an estimated tumour fraction). Parts per million (PPM) is a fraction multiplied by one million, so the number is only as meaningful as the fraction it scales: 0.01% is 100 PPM, and 0.00024% is 2.4 PPM, the lowest allele fraction Santonja and colleagues reported for ctDNA detection in breast cancer.

Concentration and fraction can move apart. If two equal one-millilitre aliquots each hold the same number of tumour molecules but one holds more background cell-free DNA, the concentration is unchanged and the fraction falls. A detection call and a reliable amount are also different claims, because the detection limit and the quantitation range are validated separately. Nothing here gives a conversion between assays: MTM/mL cannot be turned into PPM from the printed result, and a VAF of 100 PPM at one variant is not a tumour fraction of 100 PPM.

Santonja et al., EMBO Mol Med 2023: tumour-informed and tumour-naive ctDNA assays compared, allele fractions to 2.4 parts per million
FDA, Use of Circulating Tumor DNA for Curative-Intent Solid Tumor Drug Development, November 2024
Armbruster and Pry, 2008: limit of blank, detection and quantitation

notes: Method card, what it measures: the quantity an assay states, either a count of tumour-attributed molecules per volume of plasma (a concentration), a share of a named total (a fraction), or a call. How: sequencing or PCR on one finite plasma aliquot, then a calculation the laboratory defines. Keep the unit, the denominator and the assay version attached to every value.

Table, MTM/mL: mean tumour molecules per millilitre of plasma under the assay's own calculation across its tracked features. Boundary: a concentration estimated from tracked features, not the number of cancer cells per millilitre and not a share of anything.

Table, PPM: parts per million, a fraction multiplied by one million, so 1 PPM is 0.0001% and 100 PPM is 0.01%. Boundary: name the fraction being scaled, because 100 PPM of variant alleles, of evaluated DNA and of tumour-attributed molecules are three different claims.

Table, variant allele fraction: the share of evaluated alleles at one position that carry a stated variant. Boundary: it depends on copy number, on which clones carry the variant and on the measurement, and a variant present in a blood-cell clone counts the same way as one from a tumour.

Table, tumour fraction: an estimated share of evaluated DNA attributable to tumour. Boundary: it is a model output that rests on the method and its calibration, and it is not automatically any single variant's VAF.

Fictional arithmetic, concentration against fraction: two equal 1 mL aliquots each hold 4 tumour-attributed molecules. Aliquot A also holds 16 background molecules, so 4 of 20 is 20% and the concentration is 4 molecules per mL. Aliquot B holds 36 background molecules, so 4 of 40 is 10% and the concentration is still 4 per mL. More background lowered the fraction and left the concentration alone. These toy shares are not a VAF, an estimated tumour fraction or MTM/mL.

Fictional arithmetic, rescaling: a VAF of 0.01% at Variant R equals 100 PPM of variant-supporting alleles. That does not make a tumour fraction of 100 PPM, and a second report of 0.2 MTM/mL is a concentration, so 100 and 0.2 cannot be compared or converted without the methods and calibration of both assays.

Method limit, detection against quantitation: a qualifying detection call and a reliable numerical amount have separate validation criteria. A detected value below the validated quantitative range does not support an exact fold change, and extra decimal places do not create precision.

Method limit, finite input: the plasma volume drawn is not the volume or the number of molecules recovered and evaluated. Low molecular counts, changes in background DNA, poor recovery or incompatible calibration all limit comparison across assays, and a printed zero is not a count of zero cancer cells anywhere in the body.

Evidence read: in Magbanua's 84-patient pilot of neoadjuvant treatment, ctDNA in MTM/mL was correlated with MRI functional tumour volume at every time point (Spearman rho 0.42 to 0.49). Santonja's comparison reported allele fractions down to 2.4 PPM for hybrid-capture sequencing of 1,347 to 7,491 tumour-identified mutations and 4.7 PPM for multiplex PCR of 21 to 47 structural variants. Each figure belongs to its assay and cohort.

A trend also needs the collection time, treatment context, assay version and quantitative range. In its November 2024 drug-development guidance, FDA asks for precision, accuracy and detection-limit evaluation across relevant inputs and cut-offs, using representative clinical specimens and appropriately comparable reference material. A printed number below another assay's nominal detection limit does not establish that the other assay would miss that sample: the measured quantity, specimen, input, recovery and calling rules may differ. A reference-material result is not automatically a clinical sensitivity estimate.

Consider a fictional assay estimating tumour fraction at 6 parts per million (PPM) and then 2 PPM. Both samples are called detected, but the second is below the assay's reliable quantitation range. The printed estimates fall by two-thirds; they do not establish that the cancer volume fell by two-thirds. Retain the qualifying calls and uncertainty, because shedding and background DNA can change the signal. A second method reporting molecules per millilitre cannot simply be placed on this fraction scale. Even a matching unit label does not establish matching calibration. Keeping serial methods and input comparable helps interpretation without removing biological variation.

The blank, detection and quantitation limits answer different questions. The blank limit is the highest apparent analyte concentration expected from replicate samples with no analyte; the detection limit is the lowest concentration reliably distinguished from that background; the quantitation limit is the lowest concentration meeting predefined bias and imprecision goals (Armbruster and Pry, 2008). Quantitation and detection limits may coincide or differ. A qualifying detection below a validated quantitative range supports presence more strongly than an exact fold change. For a read-based variant allele fraction, the denominator is informative reads covering that locus, not cancer cells or plasma volume; keep a molecule-based method's own definition instead.

records.name: Tumour-infiltrating lymphocytes (TILs)
records.tldr: Tumour-infiltrating lymphocytes are lymphocytes found in tumour tissue. Their identity, location, measurement denominator and function answer different questions.
records.summary: Tumour-infiltrating lymphocytes (TILs) are lymphocytes found in sampled tumour tissue, including T- and B-cell populations. The breast stromal TIL method estimates the area occupied by a defined mononuclear inflammatory infiltrate within eligible tumour-associated stroma on H&E sections. Higher pretreatment scores were associated with better outcomes in the cited early triple-negative breast cancer cohorts, but those associations do not guarantee an individual outcome or establish extra benefit from pembrolizumab. Intratumoral location, stromal area, immune-cell counts and cells expanded for TIL therapy are different measurements or uses.

notes: The breast stromal TIL method estimates the area occupied by mononuclear inflammatory cells, including lymphocytes and plasma cells, as a percentage of eligible tumour-associated stroma. It is not the percentage of all cells, a CD8-cell count or the fraction of cancer cells being killed.

Define the eligible region and treatment setting before estimating the percentage. Use the specified exclusions for normal structures, in-situ disease, necrosis, crush damage and biopsy-site changes, and assess the region overall rather than only its hottest spot. A prognostic association does not establish added benefit from a particular treatment.

In the pooled analysis of 2,148 early-stage TNBC patients given anthracycline-based chemotherapy with or without taxanes, each 10 percentage-point increase in pretreatment stromal TILs corresponded to an adjusted invasive disease-free survival hazard ratio of 0.87 (95% confidence interval 0.83 to 0.91) and overall survival hazard ratio of 0.84 (0.79 to 0.89). These associations do not establish an added pembrolizumab benefit by TIL level.

Among 906 TNBC patients from six neoadjuvant chemotherapy trials, pathological complete response occurred in 80 of 260 with low TILs (0% to 10%), 117 of 373 with intermediate TILs (11% to 59%) and 136 of 273 with high TILs (at least 60%): about 31%, 31% and 50%. These categories describe that analysis and are not universal treatment cutoffs.

Fictional area exercise: region A has 4 units of eligible stroma with 0.4 occupied by infiltrate; region B has 1 unit with 0.6 occupied. Pooled occupied area is (0.4 + 0.6)/(4 + 1) = 20%. Averaging the regional percentages without area weighting gives (10% + 60%)/2 = 35%. This arithmetic illustrates the denominator; it does not prescribe a pixel workflow for clinical semiquantitative scoring.

A fictional sTIL estimate of 30% means that the defined mononuclear infiltrate occupies about 30% of eligible stromal area. It does not mean 30% of all cells are lymphocytes or CD8 cells, or that 30% of cancer cells are being killed. Intratumoral TILs, positive-nucleus fractions, cells per square millimetre and bulk immune RNA measure different things. Additional stains change the measurement rather than silently changing its denominator.

Residual-disease recommendations assess the residual tumour bed rather than simply reusing untreated invasive borders. Keep specimen type, site, treatment setting and observer calibration. A high score does not prove tumour-specific recognition, entry into every malignant nest or a permanent hot-tumour state.

To interpret a stromal TIL estimate, retain the block, sampled site, specimen type and treatment setting, then define the eligible stromal region and its exclusions. The output is a continuous estimated percentage of that area occupied by the specified infiltrate. State whether a trained observer or a computational method produced it, with calibration and regional sampling where relevant. Artifacts, sparse stroma, heterogeneity, observer variation and an unrepresentative sample can limit the result. The section uses finite tissue, and measurement reproducibility is a separate question from validation for clinical treatment selection.

TIL is a location label, CD8 is a phenotype and antigen specificity is another property. Simoni found bystander CD8 cells recognizing viral rather than cancer epitopes in human lung and colorectal tumours; the study’s CD39 associations are not a universal test of every cell’s target. A functional assay compares defined effectors and targets with recognition and target-survival controls. Neither presence, cytokine release nor one killing assay reproduces every access barrier or establishes clinical benefit.

The Loi analysis pooled nine studies. In its node-negative subgroup with at least 30% stromal TILs, three-year overall survival was 99% (95% CI 97% to 100%) after the specified adjuvant chemotherapy. Denkert’s pooled neoadjuvant population contained 3,771 patients overall, including the 906 TNBC patients described above. These population and subgroup findings do not make the study categories universal beneficial-TIL thresholds or establish additional pembrolizumab benefit by score.

In a fictional section, 0.4 square millimetres of mononuclear infiltrate within 2 square millimetres of eligible stroma gives 20% by area. Separately, 30 CD8 cells among 100 counted lymphocytes gives 30% of those counted lymphocytes. Neither is the fraction of all tumour cells, a measure of cancer specificity or evidence of useful killing. One occupied unit among five equal eligible stromal-area units also gives 20%; the drawing illustrates a denominator rather than prescribing pixel counting for semiquantitative breast scoring.

Fixed sections and morphology or selected stains can measure identity, compartment and abundance; viable-cell assays ask about phenotype and function. Dissociation loses native location, culture can select populations and tests consume finite material. Keep cells per square millimetre, specified cell fractions, stromal-area percentages and assay-specific function distinct. TIL therapy is a manufactured expanded-cell product: a tissue count does not establish product yield, composition, potency or treatment success. Sampling, damage, mixed compartments, unsuitable markers and culture selection are different failure modes, and descriptive pathology, research function and clinical treatment selection require different validation.

records.name: Immunohistochemistry (IHC)
records.tldr: Staining a tissue slice with antibodies so a protein shows up in colour under the microscope.
records.summary: Immunohistochemistry (IHC) uses antibody binding and signal development to show a selected protein in a prepared tissue section. Interpretation retains which cells and compartments stain, the intensity and distribution, and the named marker-specific method. A percentage, intensity category or composite score can describe different aspects of the result. Fixation, retrieval, controls, sampling and observer variation affect interpretation. Automated quantification also needs validation for its marker, specimens and intended use. A research stain or generic score does not replace a validated clinical selection assay.

notes: There is no universal IHC scoring scale or positivity threshold. Retain antibody clone, retrieval and detection method, controls, eligible cells, subcellular location, intensity, distribution and intended use. A research stain does not automatically replace a clinical selection assay.

An H-score under the intensity-weighted convention is weak-cell percentage plus twice moderate-cell percentage plus three times strong-cell percentage, on a 0 to 300 scale. Fictional example: 50 unstained, 10 weak, 20 moderate and 20 strong cells out of 100 give 50% positive and H-score 110. Neither is a molecule count.

Bulk receptor abundance and staining mainly on blood vessels can both be correct: one measures a mixture and the other locates signal. Neither establishes target accessibility or treatment benefit. Staining also does not establish protein activity or cancer-cell dependence on that protein.

IHC makes selected proteins visible through antibody binding and signal development in a prepared section. Specificity, retrieval, detection, positive controls, internal controls and background matter. Nuclear and membrane signals answer different questions. Multiplex fluorescence adds markers but still needs validated antibody performance and cell-boundary assignment.

In the conventional Allred scheme, proportion categories are 0 for no positive cells, 1 for less than 1%, 2 for 1% to 10%, 3 for 11% to 33%, 4 for 34% to 66% and 5 for 67% to 100%. Intensity is 0 for absent staining or 1, 2 and 3 for weak, moderate and strong staining. The total is 0 or 2 to 8. In a fictional separate example, 30% positive cells with moderate staining give 3 + 2 = 5. These integer bins are a named convention, not a universal positivity rule.

Equal H-scores can conceal different intensity distributions. A negative clinical category does not establish zero protein molecules. HER2 and hormone-receptor assays have marker-specific reporting rules; current CAP breast reporting retains percentage and intensity even when an optional composite score is given.

A useful IHC result identifies the block, fixation and section, antibody clone, retrieval and detection system, eligible cells and scored compartment. Cutting and staining use finite tissue. Report the percentage, intensity, location and named scoring scale, together with expected-positive tissue, relevant internal controls and background assessment. Poor preservation, nonspecific binding, few eligible cells, heterogeneous staining and observer variation can limit interpretation. Validation must fit the assay and its intended use; a research measurement is not automatically a clinical selection test.

Staining recognises an antibody-defined molecular feature, or epitope, rather than automatically proving a complete functioning protein. In an invented repair-gene example, weaker staining in identified cancer cells than in normal neighbours supports a cell-specific signal difference if the controls are adequate. The antibody may recognise a fragment or more than one protein form, so this does not give the amount of intact useful repair protein. The relevant form and current repair need suitable measurements of their own. One validated method can sometimes answer several questions, but measuring one property does not establish every other one.

records.name: Multiplex immunofluorescence
records.tldr: This approach measures several protein markers in a tissue section, in one or more imaging cycles. Image analysis then estimates cells, counts and distances under defined rules.
records.summary: Multiplex immunofluorescence measures selected protein-marker signals in a tissue section, using one or several imaging cycles. Cyclic methods build a high-plex image of one section by repeating staining, imaging and signal removal and then registering the cycles: t-CyCIF produced up to 60-plex images of formalin-fixed specimens and showed that antigenicity changes with cycle number (Lin and colleagues, 2018), and IBEX imaged more than 65 parameters in one section by iterative staining and chemical bleaching (Radtke and colleagues, 2020). A six-institution study of a six-plex PD-1 and PD-L1 panel, imaged with a locked-down image analysis algorithm, reported average intersite concordance of cell densities of R squared 0.75 in breast carcinoma and 0.72 in non-small cell lung cancer tissue microarrays (Taube and colleagues, 2021); that is reproducibility for one specified panel and workflow, not for multiplex immunofluorescence in general. A cell phenotype is a rule-based call from the measured panel, a density needs a stated denominator, and a distance needs a stated definition (cell centre or cell boundary).

notes: Assay card for multiplex immunofluorescence (a reading guide, not a score). Input and tissue cost: a compatible fixed or frozen section; staining uses material and may involve repeated processing, and the section does not preserve viable cells for a killing assay. Output and units: marker images, fluorescence intensity in assay-dependent units, cell counts, cells per square millimetre, cell fractions and defined distances in micrometres. Controls: marker-positive and marker-negative material, comparison with validated single-marker staining, channel or spectral controls, background assessment, cycle alignment and boundary overlays. Thresholds: panel-specific marker and phenotype rules locked before the intended comparison and tested for reproducibility. Failure modes: autofluorescence, overlapping signals, nonspecific antibodies, staining-order effects, tissue loss, alignment errors and incorrect cell boundaries. Cannot establish: all proteins, live-cell behaviour, antigen specificity, actual killing or universal treatment eligibility. Validation: specific to the panel, staining, imaging, analysis and intended use.

Figure reading (fictional, no cutoff): channels A and B are measured, registered marker images; the overlay adds estimated cell masks. Centre-to-centre distance includes the cell interiors, while boundary-to-boundary distance spans only the gap, so the two rulers give different numbers for the same pair. Proximity under either rule is not contact, recognition or killing.

records.tldr: Single-cell and single-nucleus RNA sequencing profile captured messages assigned to recovered cells or nuclei.
records.summary: RNA is distributed across cellular compartments. Whole-cell and nucleus preparations sample different material and can recover different populations. Barcodes label captured profiles rather than certifying one intact cell; quality, ambient RNA and doublet checks remain necessary. Sparse capture and selective recovery prevent a complete census, and many profiles from one biopsy do not create independent patient replicates.

Dissociation can lose fragile cells; nuclei can come from frozen tissue; fixed-material probe methods count ligated probes and cannot reveal every variant or splice product.
A zero can be a missed molecule (dropout) rather than absence; ambient RNA contaminates profiles; a doublet combines cells or nuclei; correction does not certify every barcode.
A cluster groups similar profiles and does not prove malignancy, lineage or a clone; cancer-cell identification needs supporting evidence.
Thousands of cells from one biopsy are nested in one biological sample; splitting into two libraries does not create two patients; replicate-level aggregation is one approach.

Record compatible viable/frozen/fixed preparation, material used, chemistry, cell/nucleus recovery and quality/identity checks. Report a gene-by-barcode table with its UMI/read/probe counting unit. Cell calling, low-quality and doublet criteria are chemistry/version-specific. Selective recovery, sparse capture, ambient RNA, degradation and batch require validation; a platform name provides neither a complete census nor clinical validity.

A detection fraction uses the analysed profiles and a stated detection rule: it is not automatically the fraction of all cells in the original tissue. A profile with one immune-gene count but otherwise epithelial features is not thereby identified as an immune cell. Sparse recovery, ambient RNA and more than one contributing cell can complicate its interpretation. Check coherent marker evidence and the method of assignment; a mixture of markers does not by itself establish a new cell type. Pooling the counts from a selected set of profiles is pseudobulk. Five hundred nuclei from one biopsy can summarize that selected population, while the biopsy remains one biological specimen rather than five hundred independent patients.

Background correction estimates which part of a profile comes from free RNA in the preparation. SoupX's authors discuss deliberately overcorrecting contamination at the cost of removing a small amount of genuine signal. The estimated contamination and settings therefore need review; a corrected weak count or zero is not an infallible label of the molecule's origin.

Residual tumour here means cancer remaining in the sampled tissue after treatment. For residual-tumour research, first support malignant-cell identity, then ask which recovered states, target messages and immune profiles are present. A stress programme does not establish a genetic clone or explain survival. In Kim and colleagues' twenty-person triple-negative breast-cancer study, longitudinal exome data and single-cell DNA/RNA data in eight participants supported selection of pre-existing genotypes alongside expression reprogramming under the studied treatment. This is not a universal resistance mechanism. Compare the sampled region, time, preparation, recovery and analysis before attributing a difference to treatment; a missing cluster need not have been eliminated. In a separate fictional calculation, an input suspension truly containing 4 percent malignant nuclei gives an expectation of 240 among 6,000 retained profiles only if malignant and other nuclei have equal inclusion through recovery, capture and quality filtering. Tissue-area cellularity is a different denominator. The calculation is neither a yield forecast nor an adequacy cutoff.

records.name: Spatial transcriptomics
records.tldr: These methods measure RNA signals while keeping information about position in a tissue section. A measured spot, an estimated cell boundary and an imputed value are different kinds of evidence.
records.summary: Spatial transcriptomics measures RNA signals while retaining information about where they came from in a tissue section. Sequencing capture and imaging-based detection use different measurement units. A third approach, region-of-interest profiling such as digital spatial profiling, releases oligonucleotide tags only from regions an operator chooses; the method paper describes regions covering 1 to about 5,000 cells and panels of up to 44 proteins, or 1,412 genes with sequencing readout, on formalin-fixed tissue (Merritt and colleagues, 2020), so the result depends on how the regions were selected. The original sequencing-based method placed sections on arrays of positionally barcoded primers and kept two-dimensional position (Ståhl and colleagues, 2016); a capture spot is a positional barcode and can span several cells. MERFISH imaged 100 to 1,000 RNA species chosen by probe design (Chen and colleagues, 2015), a targeted gene set and not every transcript. Assigning molecules to cells depends on estimated cell boundaries: many methods approximate cell positions from nuclear stains, and distinguishing the boundaries of individual cells is challenging and can hamper downstream analysis; Baysor was developed to optimise boundaries from transcript composition and cell morphology (Petukhov and colleagues, 2022). Gene values imputed by aligning single-cell data to a spatial map, as Tangram does (shown in mouse brain; Biancalani and colleagues, 2021), are model outputs and not extra RNA molecules detected by the spatial assay.

Failure modes: poor RNA, incomplete probe coverage, low capture, image-registration errors, inaccurate segmentation, spillover and unsuitable reference models. Limits: no automatic single-cell identity, complete transcriptome, whole-tumour representation, proven interaction or clinical selection rule. Validation tier: many workflows are research methods, so check analytical and intended-use validation for the exact assay and model; resolution claims and regulatory status are separate questions.

records.name: Cell composition confound (tumour versus stroma and immune cells)
records.tldr: Because a tumour sample is a mix of cancer, stromal and immune cells, a difference between two samples may only reflect a different mix of cells.
records.summary:
A tumour specimen can contain malignant, immune, stromal and normal cells. A difference in an aggregate molecular signal can reflect a changed mixture, changed expression within cells or both. That is different from a directly counted cell fraction or a density per sampled area, each of which also needs its denominator and sampled region.

Preparation can change what is recovered. Slyper and colleagues compared single-cell and single-nucleus profiling in matched tumour specimens and found similar cell types at sometimes different proportions. A recovered profile mixture is therefore not automatically the original tissue census. Deconvolution and purity models can help investigate contributions under assumptions; they do not certify the cell of origin of every signal or remove sampling differences.

notes: In a fictional assay using equal sampled areas and the same counting method, ten immune cells among fifty total cells is 20%, while ten among twenty is 50%. The immune count remains ten. Loss of other cells can raise the fraction without additional immune-cell entry; these observations alone do not establish recruitment, recognition or killing. This simple cell fraction is not the clinical stromal tumour-infiltrating-lymphocyte score, which has a different denominator.

A second invented comparison starts with ten cells in one square millimetre of viable edge from lesion L. Follow-up A counts ten in the same stated area and region of L, giving ten cells per square millimetre at both times under the supplied assumptions. Follow-up B counts ten in 0.2 square millimetres from an injured centre of lesion M, giving fifty per square millimetre. B does not show a rise within L. Retain the lesion, viable area, centre or edge, collection time, treatment context and counting method. An early sample can capture transient injury signals and a later one a changed surviving-cell mixture. Equal area does not make separate tissue pieces identical, and matched sampling alone still cannot establish recruitment causation.

Measurement layers ask different questions. Anatomical imaging describes structure; tracer imaging depends on the stated product and its distribution; immunohistochemistry localises a protein in sampled tissue; bulk RNA pools captured messages; receptor sequencing describes recovered sequences and their sampled abundances; and controlled recognition or killing assays test a specified function under their conditions. RNA abundance is not accessible surface protein. Formenti's lung-cancer radiation-plus-ipilimumab study used clinical, blood-repertoire and selected functional readouts together; none is a universal immune-success marker or a substitute for the other measurements.

records.name: T-cell states
records.tldr: Response history and measured function help describe a T cell's state. One marker cannot provide a complete label.
records.summary:
Naive, effector, memory and exhausted populations describe response histories and differentiation programmes, not one mandatory sequence for every T cell. Anergy and exhaustion are distinct mechanisms. Regulatory function is a separate role. Identity, location, receptor specificity, state and measured function are complementary observations.

In chronic viral infection in mice, TCF1-associated progenitor populations sustained responses and supplied the proliferative burst after PD-1 blockade. In tumour models, progenitor exhausted cells differed from terminally exhausted cells; the related melanoma observations were associations rather than a universal treatment-selection rule. Progenitor-like exhaustion is not ordinary memory. A shared receptor does not require a shared functional phenotype, and PD-1 or TCF1 alone does not establish state or tumour specificity.

Paired human skin-cancer biopsies after PD-1 blockade showed expanded clonotypes not previously observed in the same tumour, supporting clonal replacement as another response model. Absence from an earlier sample does not establish absence throughout the body. A fictional PD-1-positive population near cancer can include viral-reactive and tumour-peptide-reactive cells. Neither proximity nor peptide response proves natural tumour recognition or killing. Preserve response history, sampling site, time, multiple markers and controlled function; neither division nor a favourable pattern predicts individual benefit.

notes: Naive describes absence of initial antigen-driven activation, not recent thymic birth. Effector denotes developed response functions, including help or killing; memory can support renewed responses but promises neither permanent protection nor cancer specificity. State categories are not one mandatory developmental trajectory. Anergy, exhaustion, external suppression and regulatory role remain distinct.

The same paired receptor can occur with different functional phenotypes and response histories. Fictional R1 memory-associated and progenitor-like exhausted observations are separate observations, not a measured transition. Progenitor-like exhaustion is distinct from ordinary memory; shared TCF1 or division does not make their programmes equivalent.

Two fictional six-symbol PD-1-positive populations near cancer have different controlled peptide responses: one viral and one tumour-peptide directed. Marker and proximity do not establish specificity; peptide response does not establish natural tumour display, access or killing. Checkpoint blockade does not rewrite receptor specificity. Preserve tissue, sampling time, population definitions and controlled function alongside RNA/protein panels; favourable markers or division alone cannot predict benefit.

Source scope: teaching synthesis checked against the cited abstracts and specified accessible primary text on 9 November 2026; fictional examples are not clinical observations or treatment-selection rules.

In Burger and colleagues' engineered mouse lung tumours, the subdominant response contained heterogeneous TCF1-positive populations, including a CCR6/Tc17-associated subset that did not preferentially benefit from checkpoint blockade. Long-peptide vaccination with the two model antigens and cyclic di-GMP improved the subdominant response; a subdominant-only arm also tested antigen-specific effects. The separate human analyses were associations, not a validated universal TCF1/CCR6 requirement, target-deletion rule or clone-pruning instruction.

Reduced division and immediate effector activity are separate measurements. In healthy-donor CD8 subsets, Henson and colleagues measured reduced proliferation alongside cytokine, perforin and granzyme expression; that protein panel alone is not a direct target-death assay, and not every EMRA cell carried the measured senescence markers. Pereira and colleagues separately demonstrated killing by defined senescent-like CD27-negative/CD28-negative CD8 cells, including MHC-I-deficient targets and NKG2D-DAP12-associated NK-like activity. These observations do not establish conventional tumour-specific TCR killing, durable control or clinical benefit for every highly differentiated cell.

records.name: Flow cytometry (immunophenotyping)
records.tldr: A machine that streams cells one by one past lasers and reads the surface proteins (CD markers) each carries, identifying what kind of cell it is. It is how leukaemias and lymphomas are typed and how residual disease is counted.
records.summary: Antibodies tagged with fluorescent dyes label CD19, CD20, CD33, CD34, CD38, BCMA and dozens of other markers; the pattern (immunophenotype) distinguishes B from T from myeloid lineages and normal from malignant cells. It diagnoses acute leukaemia, CLL and myeloma from blood or marrow within hours, and multiparameter or next-generation flow measures minimal residual disease to one cell in 100,000-1,000,000, guiding transplant and maintenance decisions. It also confirms that a CAR-T target (CD19, BCMA) is still present after relapse, since antigen loss is a recognised escape.

notes: Denominators, fictional arithmetic: a run records 12,000 events, and after excluding debris, cell pairs and dead-cell events 10,000 recovered gated cells remain, of which 1,000 are T-cell events and 100 bind a reagent. Binding is 100 / 1,000 = 10% of the T-cell parent, 100 / 10,000 = 1% of recovered cells and 100 / 12,000 = 0.83% of recorded events. All three are correct for their own question and exchanging them changes the claim. Nested gates show membership and not area, no cells per millilitre or whole-body total follows, and binding or marker identity does not show killing.

Method card, what it measures: light scatter and fluorescence from individual events in a prepared cell suspension, grouped by a chosen panel of stains. Input: whole blood, isolated cells or dissociated tissue, where preparation and staining use a defined aliquot and compatibility with later assays depends on fixation and other processing and tissue dissociation removes geography and can recover cell types unevenly. Output: event counts, percent of a named parent population, fluorescence in instrument-dependent units, and cells per volume only with a validated counting method. Controls: instrument checks, unstained and single-stain controls, viability, biological controls and fluorescence-minus-one controls for hard boundaries. Failure modes: dead cells, aggregates, weak markers, nonspecific staining, signal overlap, cell loss and inconsistent gates. It cannot tell unmeasured proteins, original tissue position, antigen specificity from general markers or benefit.

What compensation does and does not do: in multicolour analysis spectral overlap between detectors needs compensation, and a mathematical and experimental analysis showed that photon-counting statistics add a nonlinear error to compensated parameters while measurement and log-scale binning errors add linear ones, most visibly with red and far-red fluorochromes where less light is emitted (Roederer 2001). Compensation or spectral unmixing therefore corrects overlap and does not repair a poorly chosen stain or set a positivity gate. The community guidelines (Cossarizza 2021) are methods guidance on preparation, panels and analysis and give no universal immune-response cut-off. A degranulation marker on the cell surface is an activity readout that accompanied cytolysis in antigen-specific CD8 T cells and is not itself measured target-cell death (Betts 2003).

Gating is selection within recorded data, not physical collection. A typical analysis checks acquisition quality, excludes debris and cell pairs, assesses viability where the assay requires it, and identifies populations with a stated marker panel. Intracellular assays may assess viability before fixation; not every flow experiment studies living cells. Fluorescence-minus-one controls omit one stain while retaining the others and can help place a boundary, but do not establish antibody specificity. Tight earlier gates can discard unexpected or rare populations. Automated clusters still need biological and technical checks (Cossarizza 2021). A cell sorter can physically collect selected events for downstream work, subject to recovery, purity and functional-viability requirements; an analytical gate alone does not do this (Cossarizza 2019).

Absolute counts need a documented counting method, such as a suitable counting-bead standard or an instrument with validated absolute-count capability, with specimen volume and dilution retained. Counts of recorded events, percentages of a gate and cells per original blood volume are different outputs. The 2021 community guidelines describe both bead-based and instrument-based counting in specific protocols; neither makes every marker panel a validated clinical test.

Scatter and marker panels help define populations under the stated assay, but scatter alone does not uniquely identify a cell type. Low event numbers and rare populations need uncertainty and acceptance rules appropriate to the panel and purpose. A gate boundary, minimum event count or research cluster is not a universal clinical-response threshold, and analytical reproducibility of the panel does not establish treatment benefit.

records.name: Cytokine
records.tldr: Small proteins immune cells use to talk to each other: alarms, recruitment calls, growth orders and stand-down signals. Some are cancer drugs, and a flood of them is the danger of certain immunotherapies.
records.summary: Interleukins, interferons, tumour necrosis factor and chemokines each act on cells carrying the matching receptor; IL-2 drives T-cell growth and was one of the first immunotherapies (aldesleukin), interferon-alpha was used in melanoma and leukaemia, and engineered cytokines aim to keep the benefit while losing the toxicity. Tumours secrete cytokines that recruit suppressive cells and drive inflammation, and IL-6 is a major driver of cancer cachexia. When CAR-T cells or T-cell engagers activate en masse they release cytokines in a surge (cytokine release syndrome), treated by blocking IL-6 with tocilizumab. A cytokine name does not specify one outcome: one cytokine can act differently on different receiving cells (pleiotropy), different signals can give overlapping outputs (redundancy), and receptor availability, concentration, exposure time and cell state all shape the response. A review of receptor biology said that all cytokines, to a greater or lesser extent, show pleiotropy (multiple biological actions) and redundancy (shared biological actions), and proposed that redundancy might be explained by related cytokines using a common receptor subunit, while pleiotropy requires that receptors exert different activities on different cells (Nicola, 1994). Different IL-2 and anti-IL-2 antibody complexes selectively expanded CD8 T cells or CD4 regulatory T cells in mice, so the formulation and the receiving cells mattered (Boyman et al., 2006). Chemokines help direct cell movement through gradients: in mouse skin an immobilised CCL21 gradient guided dendritic cells towards lymphatic vessels, and displacing or swamping it abolished directed migration (Weber et al., 2013), but movement also needs a compatible receptor and a traversable route. Measurements answer different questions: a concentration in picograms per millilitre of a named fluid, the percentage of a defined cell gate making a protein after stimulation, and RNA expression are different layers, a blood concentration does not reconstruct a tumour gradient, and two preparations can share an average (0 and 20, or 10 and 10, picograms per millilitre both average 10) while differing in spatial pattern. Intracellular cytokine staining usually involves a stimulation of a few hours (4 to 6 hours was usually sufficient to detect interferon gamma and tumour necrosis factor), a block on secretion with brefeldin A or monensin so that the protein stays inside the cell, and negative and positive controls (Cossarizza et al., 2019). Calibration and a detection limit belong in the same report; that is OnCo's reporting advice and not a finding of the cited guideline. Chemokines are a family of cytokines and not a separate category, a growth-support signal such as IL-2 does not choose the antigen a T cell recognises, and more signal is not automatically more useful or safer immunity. For interferons, timing and the receiving cell mattered in mouse experiments: endogenous type I interferon was needed to prevent the growth of carcinogen-induced and transplanted tumours and acted through host blood-lineage cells (Dunn et al., 2005), whereas prolonged interferon signalling in experimental tumours maintained a resistance programme to checkpoint blockade (Benci et al., 2016). That a signal is tumour-associated does not by itself make it a safe target; this is OnCo's boundary statement and not a cited finding.

notes: Cytokines are signalling proteins whose binding to a suitable receptor changes signalling and gene expression in a receiving cell. Autocrine action is on the producing cell, paracrine action is on neighbours, and endocrine action is at a distance, for example after entry into the circulation. Distant action is possible rather than the default for every cytokine (British Society for Immunology, Cytokines: Introduction). Chemokines are a cytokine family involved in cell recruitment and can also affect leukocyte activation (NLM MeSH, Chemokines). The information-versus-fuel distinction is a reading rule: a measured amount of signalling protein does not measure the energy available to the cell, and a message without the relevant receptor and response machinery does not establish a response.

records.name: Serial blood sampling
records.tldr: Blood can often be collected again, but every draw is a new finite specimen whose fraction, handling and collection time determine its meaning.
records.summary: Serial blood sampling can follow circulating analytes or cell populations over time. Plasma, serum and blood-cell fractions are different inputs. Circulating material does not preserve the local tissue architecture and cell relationships available from a tissue sample.

links.label: Razavi et al., matched plasma, white-cell and tumour sequencing, 2019
NCI cell-free DNA collection and processing practices

notes: Cell-free DNA includes DNA from non-malignant sources. A plasma variant can originate in a blood-cell clone; matched white-cell DNA and tumour tissue can help assess origin, without eliminating sampling uncertainty. A negative plasma result can reflect low shedding or limited assay sensitivity rather than absence of cancer.

Retain collection time, treatment context, tube, processing delay, fraction, storage, input quantity, assay and detection limit. Repeat collections have practical burdens and provide later biological time points. Comparisons require compatible methods and the same named question.

Plasma is separated from anticoagulated blood, while serum is obtained after clotting. White-cell DNA can supply a comparator; mononuclear-cell fractions support selected immune measurements; plasma proteins can come from multiple tissues. Cell-free DNA includes a tumour-derived subset, circulating tumour DNA. These fractions are not automatically interchangeable. The intended method may require whole blood or a specified separated fraction; those inputs are not automatically interchangeable.

Fictional example: a variant is found in plasma and matched white-cell DNA but not in available tumour tissue. A blood-cell clone is a possible source, alongside assay and sampling uncertainty. One tissue sample may miss a clone. Neither the plasma label nor the negative tissue result alone proves origin.

Like serial weather readings, repeated draws can follow change only when the same question and compatible methods are used. Blood immune cells are not the same population as cells inside a tumour. Low shedding, finite molecules, handling or assay sensitivity can explain a negative plasma result without proving cancer absent; repeatability does not remove collection burdens or consent requirements.

A blood assay starts with a named analyte or cell population, an appropriate collected fraction, processing and a defined measurement. Each draw and derived aliquot has finite volume; repeat draws have practical and health burdens. Outputs may be concentrations, molecule or variant estimates, or cell counts and frequencies. Input adequacy, detection limits and intended-use cutoffs belong to the assay. Wrong tubes, processing delays, cell breakdown, low input and mistaken source assignment can limit results. Monitoring, diagnostic and research uses need their own validation; a circulating result does not map tumour-wide cell composition or tissue localisation, and a negative result does not establish absence of all cancer.
